title_en: How to clear the cache on your Samsung TV
title_fa: How to clear the cache on your Samsung TV
excerpt_en: Your TV's cache is a collection of temporary files, some of which you don't need anymore. Here's why you might want to clear those out – and how.
excerpt_fa: Your TV's cache is a collection of temporary files, some of which you don't need anymore. Here's why you might want to clear those out – and how.
content_en:
How to clear the cache on your Samsung TV
If your apps or menus have been a bit sluggish, it's worth a try.
It's happened to many of us at some point. You've settled into the couch in front of your smart TV, and you just started binging your favorite show, watching that new release you've been waiting for weeks to see or anxiously anticipating the start of a big playoff game when ... your streaming app crashes.
Your first instinct may be to throw the remote across the room or immediately start browsing online for TV sales. Understandable reaction. But before you do any of that, take a deep breath and try one potential fix that could solve the problem if your TV is a Samsung: clearing the cache. Temporary cache files are stored every time you use an app, so they build up over time. The more apps you use, the more the cache grows. Eventually, that can impact your TV's performance.
Taking just a couple of minutes to clear the cache may take care of your TV's streaming issues. And don't worry, clearing your TV's cache will not delete any apps you've downloaded, mess with any of your audio/video settings, reset your Wi-Fi password or erase any software updates.
The benefits of clearing the cache on your TV
What clearing the cache on your Samsung TV will do is remove all temporary junk files that could be causing performance issues with the TV. So, if your streaming apps — like Hulu, Netflix, HBO Max, Peacock, Prime Video, YouTube and others — have been freezing or crashing when you're trying to watch them, clearing the cache may fix those issues.
Another common symptom you may encounter is extra lag or buffering as you browse through your Samsung TV menus or start up your apps; a glut of old cache data could be the culprit. Clearing it out should improve your TV's overall response time and result in smoother operation. Also worth noting is that most smart TVs have limited internal storage — typically around 8GB. However, the actual amount of available storage is far less.
For example, your Samsung TV's operating system gobbles up around 20 percent of the TV's total storage. When you factor in all the pre-installed bloatware, the apps you actually want to install and then the cache and temporary data files, there's not much storage left to spare. Clearing out all the built-up cache can free up some space to keep your apps running smoothly. Keep in mind, however, that the cache will pile up again as you continue to run apps. It's a good idea to make cache clearing a regular task every few months.
The downsides of clearing your TV's cache
There really aren't any lasting downsides to clearing your Samsung TV's cache. You're just getting rid of temporary junk files, after all. But you may experience a few minor inconveniences that are easily taken care of.
One annoyance is slower initial app loads, which occur because the app must download new temporary files (remember, you just deleted all the old ones) and images from online sources instead of loading them from the files that were locally stored on your TV. It's just a few extra seconds to wait for the first launch of each app after you cleared the cache, and subsequent launches shouldn't experience any delays.
Another small inconvenience, if you opt to Clear Data instead of Clear Cache, is the possible loss of saved app preferences, such as video playback, app layout or subtitle/closed captioning within certain apps. And you may notice within each app that some visuals like movie posters, thumbnails and other images take an extra beat to load. This happens for the same reason that the app takes an extra few seconds to launch after the TV's cache has been cleared.
How to clear your Samsung TV's cache
Clearing the cache on your Samsung smart TV is pretty quick and straightforward. And these instructions should apply to most Samsung TV models. We'll provide directions for Samsung TVs dating back to 2016 because they do vary slightly.
To clear the entire system cache for Samsung TV models made between 2020 and today, go to Settings > Support > Device Care > Start Device Care. If you want to clear the cache of individual apps, follow the same path, but choose Manage Storage rather than Start Device Care, select the app, click View Details > Clear Cache.
For 2019 and 7-Series Samsung TV models, follow Settings > Support > Self Diagnosis > TV Device Manager > Clean Now (to clear your TV's entire system), or choose an app and clear its cache from there. If you have a Samsung TV made between 2016 and 2018, you won't be able to clear caches of individual apps. But you can delete browser cookies as well as some internet data by going to Settings > Broadcasting > Expert Settings > HbbTV Settings > Delete Browsing Data.
Clearing the cache of your TV or individual apps should help with performance. If all else fails, you can always give your TV a cold boot, which works on every Samsung smart TV regardless of when it was built. With the TV on, press and hold the power button on your Samsung TV remote until the TV shuts off and turns back on. That process lasts roughly five seconds. Or, unplug the TV's power cable from the wall (or power strip), then wait 30 to 60 seconds before plugging it back in. These physical resets completely shut down the TV's operating system and clear out temporary cache files.

title_en: SpaceX successfully catches Starship after launch for the first time
title_fa: SpaceX successfully catches Starship after launch for the first time
excerpt_en: While the company has pulled off this trick a few times with Super Heavy boosters, it was a first for the Ship.
excerpt_fa: While the company has pulled off this trick a few times with Super Heavy boosters, it was a first for the Ship.
content_en:
SpaceX successfully catches Starship after launch for the first time
While the company has pulled off this trick a few times with Super Heavy boosters, it was a first for the Ship.
SpaceX nailed its first catch attempt of the Starship upper stage, safely catching the Ship with the arms of the launch tower it left from in South Texas.
SpaceX launched Starship on Friday for its 15th test flight, in which it set out to achieve some of its most ambitious goals yet. The company had planned to demonstrate its first double catch, which would see the Super Heavy V3 booster return to the launch site to be caught by the tower's chopstick arms before the upper stage, or the part known as the Ship, attempted the same landing maneuver a day later. SpaceX has caught and reflown V1 Super Heavy boosters a couple of times so far, but it hasn't yet tried to catch the Ship until now.
While Flight 15 succeeded in carrying out some of its main objectives — including deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit and catching the Ship — the first stage booster experienced a problem on its way back down to Earth and aborted its catch attempt, instead changing course to splash down in the Gulf, where it exploded before hitting the water. The Ship, though, continued on its journey in orbit for roughly 22 hours following launch before heading back down to the surface.
Mechazilla catches Starship! Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on this incredible achievement! pic.twitter.com/YJzmGUZb2B
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 14, 2026

title_en: How to clear the cache on your Xbox Series X
title_fa: How to clear the cache on your Xbox Series X
excerpt_en: Clearing the cache on your Xbox Series X can help it retain its snappiness while avoiding glitches, or you can perform a console reset if all else fails.
excerpt_fa: Clearing the cache on your Xbox Series X can help it retain its snappiness while avoiding glitches, or you can perform a console reset if all else fails.
content_en:
How to clear the cache on your Xbox Series X
Keep your Xbox Series X feeling like new by keeping your cache clear, and if that doesn't help, a reset is in order.
If you secured your Xbox Series X years before the RAM crisis made consumer tech prices skyrocket (in case you were wondering why RAM prices are so high right now), chances are it's not as lag-free as it once was. Over time, temporary files can build up in the system, leading to slowdowns and glitches. When the classic restart option doesn't suffice, consider clearing the console's cache.
Just like clearing the cache on a phone or web browser, doing so on your Xbox once in a while can help its performance while navigating between menus. Clear the cache by turning off and unplugging your Xbox Series X for two minutes, then pressing the power button multiple times before reconnecting its power cord to power-cycle the console. Power it back on, and you should be good to go.
Clearing your cache is a trick worth trying when you run into excessive loading errors or connectivity issues in your games. For instance, Epic Games notes directly on its support site that clearing the cache on an Xbox Series X can help with load failure errors in its game Rocket League.
What to expect after clearing your Xbox Series X's cache
Clearing your cache can help resolve issues if a simple restart doesn't, since this action removes files stored on the console that may have been corrupted. Other ways to help reach the expected lifespan of your Xbox Series X are to routinely clean its vents for efficient heat management and keep the console in an open area so the fan can do its job.
The console's cache is supposed to store data over time to make common routines faster by reducing the need to repeatedly load the same elements. So while it's a design choice that's supposed to help, files can still build up over months and years, clogging things up. Rest assured that clearing your cache won't affect your games or save data.
One sign that you cleared your cache correctly is when you spot the Xbox logo on the screen and the full boot process occurs. However, a Reddit user wrote that clearing the cache could temporarily increase loading times in Microsoft Flight Simulator. Then again, a user also reported quicker boot times after clearing the cache, so your experience may vary.
Consider resetting your console if issues persist
While it's a good practice to clear your console's cache once in a while, there's no specific schedule you need to maintain. Simply doing so whenever your Xbox Series X feels sluggish should do the trick.
If your current experience is abysmal, you may even want to perform a reset. Before resetting, connect your console to the internet and let your save data sync to the Xbox network. To reset the console, go to Settings > System > Console info > Reset console. You can also select the option Reset and keep my games & apps to save yourself the hassle of redownloading everything, though you'll still need to sign back into your accounts afterward.
If your console still doesn't feel as snappy as you'd like or if your games don't run as expected after wiping its cache, consider a factory reset by choosing the option Reset and remove everything in the settings. While starting fresh with a factory reset can feel like a chore since it wipes everything on the console with all unsynced data lost (considering the wait time to redownload everything, along with the other drawbacks you should know before buying an Xbox Series X), it could get your games to run smoothly so you can once again enjoy your Xbox couch sessions.

title_en: Is your car tracking your location? Here's how to check and opt out
title_fa: Is your car tracking your location? Here's how to check and opt out
excerpt_en: Modern cars are great for farming user data, and big tech companies know it. It's important to know how this information is collected and how to opt out.
excerpt_fa: Modern cars are great for farming user data, and big tech companies know it. It's important to know how this information is collected and how to opt out.
content_en:
Is your car tracking your location? Here's how to check and opt out
Where you drive is your business. Your car may disagree.
If you drive a car built sometime in the past few years, it's almost certainly tracking your location. Modern vehicles function less like cars and more like computers on wheels these days, collecting data through GPS navigation, connected services, telematics systems and manufacturer apps.
While it all started innocently enough, with manufacturers using the collected data to understand how the cars were being driven, reasons behind crashes and so on and so forth, that data has become a source of income for them. The data can be shared with insurers, marketing companies and data brokers, sometimes without explicit driver consent.
As you'd expect, it all depends on what car make, model and year you are driving. Each will collect certain information based on what sensors are available, and you'll have to dig through the menus to even be able to cancel anything. Another way to ensure your car has less info on you is to avoid pairing your phone to it, as that gives it access to your contacts, call logs, music, location and more.
That means all those useful Android Auto and CarPlay features won't be available. But at least your car will spy less on you.
How do cars collect and share location data?
GPS navigation systems are the most obvious source due to how accessible apps such as Google Maps are thanks to Android Auto, but they're far from the only one. Connected service, telematics modules and those manufacture-branded apps they shove at you when you buy a car are continuously collecting information as you drive. These often log routes, destinations and driving behaviors in the background. When you think about data privacy, you don't really think about cars as being a potential problem.
And yet, the Mozilla Foundation has ranked cars as the worst product category it has reviewed for privacy. The reason? Just how extensively major automakers collect data on where you go and how you go there. Did you brake too hard? Did you almost get in an accident? Well, all that info might end up on the desk of your insurance company, affecting how much you pay each year. This isn't just some hypothetical concern as we already know that in January 2026 the FTC banned General Motors from sharing driver location data with consumer reporting agencies after the company violated its privacy commitments.
If you're wondering just how much information your car collects on you, there are ways to find out without tearing your car apart. Services like Privacy4Cars provide a free Vehicle Privacy Report that requires you to input your car's 17-character Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) (which you can find on the dashboard or door jamb). The report will tell you what your automaker and its service providers collect, share and sell. You can also check your automaker's privacy policy or connected-services terms, plus your car's manual to figure out what data is being collected.
How to tell if your car is being tracked by GPS and how to turn it off
Even if you don't generate such a report on your car, you can dig through your car's own settings. Most manufacturers' apps and dashboard menus include a privacy or data-sharing section where you can review what's being collected. It's worth checking both the app and the infotainment system directly, since settings aren't always mirrored across both. Look for keywords like Data sharing, Connected services, Analytics, Diagnostics, Location Services, Personalization, Voice assistant, Insurance sharing, Driver monitoring, and so on. Names can vary, based on manufacturer, car make and model, and so on, but you get the gist.
Opt-out options will also differ by manufacturers. Some will allow users to opt out of data sharing through dashboard settings, while others will offer more granular control rather than an all-or-nothing switch. You do have to keep in mind that disabling tracking usually comes with trade-offs as you might end up losing roadside assistance, that beloved remote start function that lets you heat up the car before you get on in the winter, smartphone integration or other features tied to location services. Before switching everything off, you should consider what exactly you're actually willing to give up on.
One thing to keep in mind, however, is that if you're selling or trading your vehicle, you should look into erasing your data, because it won't do so automatically. You'll need to perform a factory reset on the infotainment system, remove your account and vehicle from the manufacturer's app and even notify the manufacturer of the ownership change. Skipping this step means a stranger's driving habits might impact your own insurance profile and vice versa.

The report will tell you what your automaker and its service providers collect, share and sell. You can also check your automaker's privacy policy or connected-services terms, plus your car's manual to figure out what data is being collected.
How to tell if your car is being tracked by GPS and how to turn it off
Even if you don't generate such a report on your car, you can dig through your car's own settings. Most manufacturers' apps and dashboard menus include a privacy or data-sharing section where you can review what's being collected. It's worth checking both the app and the infotainment system directly, since settings aren't always mirrored across both. Look for keywords like Data sharing, Connected services, Analytics, Diagnostics, Location Services, Personalization, Voice assistant, Insurance sharing, Driver monitoring, and so on. Names can vary, based on manufacturer, car make and model, and so on, but you get the gist.
Opt-out options will also differ by manufacturers. Some will allow users to opt out of data sharing through dashboard settings, while others will offer more granular control rather than an all-or-nothing switch. You do have to keep in mind that disabling tracking usually comes with trade-offs as you might end up losing roadside assistance, that beloved remote start function that lets you heat up the car before you get on in the winter, smartphone integration or other features tied to location services. Before switching everything off, you should consider what exactly you're actually willing to give up on.
One thing to keep in mind, however, is that if you're selling or trading your vehicle, you should look into erasing your data, because it won't do so automatically. You'll need to perform a factory reset on the infotainment system, remove your account and vehicle from the manufacturer's app and even notify the manufacturer of the ownership change. Skipping this step means a stranger's driving habits might impact your own insurance profile and vice versa.

title_en: This built-in Windows tool can diagnose your PC's battery health
title_fa: This built-in Windows tool can diagnose your PC's battery health
excerpt_en: If your laptop doesn't seem to hold a charge as well as it used to, start by checking the diagnostics this tool can report. We'll show you how to use it.
excerpt_fa: If your laptop doesn't seem to hold a charge as well as it used to, start by checking the diagnostics this tool can report. We'll show you how to use it.
content_en:
This built-in Windows tool can diagnose your PC's battery health
It's a bit hidden, but it's easy to find if you know where to look.
The health and performance of a laptop's internal components are things that are important to keep a close eye on over its lifespan. A laptop's longevity is permanently linked to the status of its battery.
If you have a laptop, the battery is one that you may want to pay particularly close attention to. A failing or struggling battery will have some significant negative impacts on your laptop's performance, in addition to eventually being the thing that stops it from booting altogether.
Thankfully, there's a nifty, little-known Windows tool that can help you diagnose your laptop battery and its condition, as well as help you to determine when it may be time for you to look at a potential replacement. Perhaps more than any other type of computer out there, laptops are exceptionally difficult to diagnose sometimes, but this built-in tool can help make your life a little bit easier.
What is Powercfg and what does it do?
In addition to its many other built-in diagnostic tools, Windows offers one that is going to be quite handy if you happen to have a laptop. It's called Powercfg, and it's one of the most powerful utilities that you can use to help figure out what's going on with your laptop's battery.
To put it simply, Powercfg will allow you to monitor and maintain the energy and systems of your computer. If you're running it on a desktop computer, it will be beneficial in allowing you to monitor the energy efficiency of your PC, as well as alter certain sleep and hibernation states.
With a laptop, however, Powercfg becomes a much more powerful and comprehensive administration utility. Though it has its uses on PC, you'll be able to feel the impact of what it can do much more clearly when you run it on a laptop.
How to run Powercfg and keep tabs on your laptop's battery
If you've been noticing your laptop acting a bit strange lately, then Powercfg may be where you want to look first. The warning signs of a dying laptop battery range from something as subtle as slower charging than normal to the more severe — like a complete, random shutdown out of nowhere. You may also notice that the laptop itself starts to bulge, indicating a swollen battery with parts that are slowly breaking down.
Running Powercfg is fairly easy even for someone who isn't a computer expert. You only need to know how to type and how to open the Terminal window as an administrator. Begin by pressing Win+X, then clicking Terminal (Admin). The window that opens is where you'll type commands to engage with Powercfg. You can also use Command Prompt, which you invoke by pressing Win+R, typing cmd in the window that appears and pressing Enter.
To start with, one of the most helpful commands to use is powercfg /batteryreport. Type that exact line into Terminal and press Enter. This will give you a complete rundown of your laptop's current status as an HTML report that will save to your computer's files. The Terminal will tell you where to locate the file. You ideally want full charge capacity to be as close to design capacity as possible, which is what the laptop was built for. A bit of wiggle room is fine, but it's worth keeping an eye on if you think your battery isn't doing so great. Anything below 40 percent needs to be replaced, according to Dell.
Powercfg /energy will run a check on your battery and the laptop's efficiency. It lasts 60 seconds and also saves as an HTML report that you can open from the location indicated. This particular command will tell you which apps and devices may need to be reconfigured due to power drain on the battery. These two commands really go a long way in allowing you to self-diagnose battery trouble, and if you discover that the battery is severely damaged or causing issues with the laptop, it's most likely time to replace it with a new one.

title_en: Tesla opens Cybercab pre-orders ‘for personal use,’ with geo restrictions and a $299 monthly fee
title_fa: Tesla opens Cybercab pre-orders ‘for personal use,’ with geo restrictions and a $299 monthly fee
excerpt_en: Even Elon Musk said the monthly fee is "too high."
excerpt_fa: Even Elon Musk said the monthly fee is "too high."
content_en:
Tesla said on Friday evening that “select customers” now have the opportunity to pre-order the company’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.”
More details became clear as those select customers looked at the order page. Tech reviewer Marques Brownlee posted that buyers “must accept delivery” in one of a handful of Texas cities and that the Cybercab will only operate in certain geofenced areas. The estimated delivery date is December 2026.
In addition to the $29,990 price tag, Cybercab owners will need to pay $299 per month to operate their vehicle.
In response to Brownlee’s post, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the Cybercab “will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval.” He added that the monthly fee is “too high”: “Should match the cost of Tesla [Full Self-Driving] and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”
Tesla’s Ashok Elluswamy offered more information about the geofencing, saying that Cybercab will work “unsupervised inside all the same geo locations as @robotaxi, just serving the owners’ needs.”
After falling far short of projected sales, Tesla recently announced it will cease Cybertruck production next year and use the additional factory capacity to build more Cybercabs.

title_en: Change these Fitbit Edge settings for a better experience
title_fa: Change these Fitbit Edge settings for a better experience
excerpt_en: The Fitbit Edge not only looks good, but packs plenty of features while remaining minimal. To get the most out of it, you only need to tweak a few settings.
excerpt_fa: The Fitbit Edge not only looks good, but packs plenty of features while remaining minimal. To get the most out of it, you only need to tweak a few settings.
content_en:
Change these Fitbit Edge settings for a better experience
How to get more out of your fitness tracker.
For a while, the Fitbit brand seemingly had its back against the wall. After Google's takeover in 2019, it released a range of branded devices, like the Sense 2 and Charge 6, but the company really started to prioritize the Pixel Watch, to the point that people began questioning whether the brand would survive.
Recently, though, Google has reaffirmed its commitment to the Fitbit name with two new devices, led by the Fitbit Edge. It's arguably one of the best fitness trackers for people who don't want to spring for a full-fledged smartwatch. It might not be on par with something like the Garmin Forerunner 570 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, but it's not trying to be.
As with any tracker, there are a variety of settings on the Edge you can change to optimize your experience, from customizing its clock through to making it a bit more deadlift-friendly. None of these tweaks are strictly necessary, but you'll probably be glad to have them ready should the need arise.
The settings that immediately improve your Edge
One of the first things you should change is your Edge's watch face, or as Google refers to it, clock face. It's not just about style — some faces support more tiles (complications or widgets) than others, letting you check stats like calorie burn and heart rate at a glance, not just the time or weather. The best ones in that regard are the Modular faces, which allow up to four or five tiles.
To browse and install faces, open Google Health, then navigate to Connections > [your device] > Watch faces > Clocks. Pick what you want, then tap Install. On your Edge, you can swap installed faces at will by tapping and holding the screen.
One tweak that's surprisingly important is Tracker Orientation, again found under device settings in the Health app. This determines whether the physical button is on the left or right relative to onscreen content. You may need to flip orientation if you find that you're accidentally hitting the button during certain activities. When deadlifting, for example, I find that the straps I wear can easily bump up against a tracker's buttons unless I wear the device higher up on my arm.
If you're syncing data with a third-party service or just want fewer distractions, it may be worth disabling Coach Insights in Google Health. In the app, go to [Profile icon] > Google Health Settings > Coaching and select No Coach Insights. That way, you won't get unprompted summaries and advice popping up on your phone during the day. These might be completely pointless if you're a fitness veteran — someone who can run a 10K or squat 400 pounds probably doesn't need to be told what their data means.
Ways to stretch out battery life on the Edge
Under device settings in Google Health, you can configure GPS settings to always use your phone for location data instead of relying on the Edge's built-in GPS. This may significantly stretch out battery life, but be warned — you won't get any location data at all if you leave your phone behind. That could be a major problem with activities where carrying your phone is impractical, like swimming. If that's a concern, it's best to leave GPS settings on Dynamic, which will flip over to built-in GPS whenever your phone is missing.
If battery life is a high priority, be sure to also leave Always-On Display off. As convenient as it is, Google notes that the feature shrinks maximum battery life from seven days to around two. Real-world performance could be less, especially if onboard GPS is running. You should definitely switch the always-on display off if you're about to run a marathon or tend to forget about charging.
Lastly, consider charging your Edge a little bit every day. When your battery is running on fumes, even five minutes of charging may be enough to restore a full day's use. For those speeds, you do need to combine your cable with a 30W power adapter, but tossing your Edge on the charger while you shower is a great way to reduce battery anxiety.

excerpt_en: "It's really happening. I promise. For real." Those are the first words from Roy Graham, Head of Story at Magic: The Gathering, in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker, the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027. An animated Magic: The Gathering series was first...

content_en:
“It’s really happening. I promise. For real.” Those are the first words from Roy Graham, Head of Story at Magic: The Gathering, in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker, the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027.
Magic: The Gathering is getting a Netflix animated series. For real this time.
Magic The Gathering: Planeswalker is set to debut on Netflix in 2027.
Magic The Gathering: Planeswalker is set to debut on Netflix in 2027.
An animated Magic: The Gathering series was first teased back in 2019 with Joe and Anthony Russo at the helm. But that fell apart. In 2024, Netflix announced it still planned to make a series based on the game, but it decided to rework it from the ground up.
Now fans are finally getting their first glimpse of the show, which will be called Planeswalker. According to the sneak peek, because each plane exists in its own pocket universe, it will have a unique design, animation, and filmmaking style.
According to a synopsis of the show shared with IGN, Planeswalker will focus on Chandra Nalaar, a “volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past.” Storyline details beyond that are vague, other than mentioning an “insidious force” that Chandra and other Planeswalkers will team up to confront “to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence.”

title_en: Got an iPhone Duo? These 9 settings make it easier to use
title_fa: Got an iPhone Duo? These 9 settings make it easier to use
excerpt_en: From Touch ID shortcuts to smarter volume buttons and camera tricks, these tweaks make Apple's foldable iPhone easier to use every day.
excerpt_fa: From Touch ID shortcuts to smarter volume buttons and camera tricks, these tweaks make Apple's foldable iPhone easier to use every day.
content_en:
Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has proven popular enough that the company can’t keep the device in stock. While the Duo introduces a new way to use an iPhone, getting the most out of this initial version may require adjusting a few settings to make it work better when it comes to everyday tasks, like unlocking the device with Touch ID, navigating the interface, and taking photos.
After spending some time with the Duo, we’d recommend making the following adjustments to make the new iPhone a bit easier to use, most notably when it comes to the use of Touch ID.
Settings to make it easier to live with Touch ID
Unlike modern iPhones, the Duo doesn’t support Face ID. That means you have to adjust to pressing a finger on the side of the device once again to authenticate with apps, unlock the device, and use Apple Pay. But there are a few things you can do to make the switch back to the older technology a bit less painful.
- Register extra fingerprints: This may seem like an obvious suggestion, but if you’re used to just registering a fingerprint or two with Touch ID, prepare to rethink that strategy with the Duo. Because the device can be held in multiple orientations, flipped both horizontally and vertically, and because of the small size of the Duo’s screen, you may find that a lot of your fingers (and thumbs!) can now reach the Touch ID button. We’d recommend holding the device in your hand and turning it in different ways, then register the fingerprints where you end up holding the device the most — on both hands. Yes, setting up Touch ID can be a bit tedious compared with Face ID, as there are multiple prints to register. Still, it’s a one-time setup, and later on you’ll be glad that you took the time to make more of your fingerprints work. To register a fingerprint, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Add a Fingerprint.
- Unlock with Apple Watch: If you’re in the market for the iPhone Duo, there’s a good likelihood that you own other Apple devices, like the Apple Watch. If that’s the case, you’re in luck because you can use your Watch to unlock the Duo without having to bother with Touch ID. This will save you time and frustration in the long run, so get used to wearing your Apple Watch more often, especially when you’re out and about and don’t want to fiddle as much with finger placement. To use the Apple Watch unlock, your watch will need to be passcode-protected and worn near your phone. To turn this feature on, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Unlock with Apple Watch.
- Rest finger to Open: This is an optional setting, not necessarily a “must” like the above, but we’ve found it useful. The “rest finger” setting is actually an accessibility feature, but it can double as a usability feature, too. When enabled, you only have to rest your finger lightly on the Touch ID sensor to unlock the device, instead of having to press down. Those who prefer this setting find it can make unlocking the phone faster and more convenient, but others may disagree, as they like the more tactile sensation of a button press. Try it both ways and see which one fits you best. To enable this one, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Rest Finger to Open.
Usability Improvements
There are a few settings that could also improve your experience with the iPhone Duo, as they may make it easier to perform certain everyday tasks, like taking screenshots or reaching different parts of the screen, among other things.
- Turn off Fixed Volume Controls: This is a favorite hack for new Duo owners, as it makes using the device in any orientation much easier. By default, the iPhone Duo’s volume buttons are “fixed,” which means that no matter how you rotate the device, the Volume Up button remains the button that increases the volume and the Volume Down button decreases it. But many people find it’s easier if the buttons’ functionality rotates with the device. That is, the buttons re-orient themselves based on how you are holding the phone, making the “up” option always on the top or right. As you fold, unfold, and flip the phone, having buttons that flip with you actually makes more sense. To turn off the fixed volume controls, go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Fixed Position Volume Controls.
- Back Tap for Screenshots: The Duo tries to make it easier to take a screenshot by pressing the side button and either the Volume Up or Volume Down button at the same time. However, you still might find the process a two-handed affair (unless you just ask Siri to do it for you). That’s why many Duo owners are turning to a buried Accessibility feature to make taking screenshots a bit less complicated. In the phone’s accessibility settings, you can configure whether a double tap or triple tap on the back of the device triggers a particular action — which you can set to ‘take a screenshot.’ (Some people prefer the triple tap so they don’t accidentally trigger the feature.) Once enabled, you could hold your Duo in one hand, then use a finger to tap on the back of the phone to take the screenshot, saving you a bit of the hassle that comes with managing the button combinations. To configure this, go to Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Back Tap > then choose a double or triple tap and your action. (Screenshot is under the “Device” menu.)
- Reachability: This is another accessibility feature that some Duo owners like to configure, but others like to have off. The option was originally designed to make larger-screened devices easier to use with one hand, which makes it sometimes hard to reach, depending on your hand size. Typically, when Reachability is turned on, the iPhone will lower the top half of the screen to make it easier to reach with your thumb. The Duo does things a little differently, though. Because the phone is wide — it’s shaped like a passport — it’s the far side of the screen that’s harder to reach than the top. So when you turn on Reachability, you will instead be able to swipe the left or right edge of the...

title_en: Transportation secretary blames ‘routine’ equipment upgrade for grounding flights nationwide
title_fa: Transportation secretary blames ‘routine’ equipment upgrade for grounding flights nationwide
excerpt_en: FAA administrator Bryan Bedford also said there's "zero evidence of anything AI-related."
excerpt_fa: FAA administrator Bryan Bedford also said there's "zero evidence of anything AI-related."
content_en:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a nationwide ground stop halting flights across the United States was caused by seemingly routine maintenance work.
Duffy said that during “routine maintenance,” copper wire at a remote location was upgraded to fiber optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. After the upgrade, a router overloaded a critical communication system, leading to the ground stop.
“It’s pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location,” Duffy said during a Saturday press conference that appeared to have technical issues of its own. “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning, was it user error or [installer] error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?”
The FAA’s acting CTO Rebecca Guy added, “When we started to see the occurrence where our network was having instability, we started to look at what was the cause. And as such, we saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate — a thousand connections over every four to five seconds.”
Guy said the FAA disabled “both of those, right away and were able to stabilize our network,” and is now performing a root cause analysis.
Duffy has repeatedly insisted, at multiple press conferences, that Congress needs to provide more funding for aviation equipment upgrades. Asked why the upgrades were made at 3pm on a Friday afternoon — rather than, say, at midnight on a Saturday — he responded that while “switchovers” at bigger airports will take place late at night, remote switchovers happen during the day.
“There will be reevaluation of when we do this work,” he said.
This was only the third nationwide ground stop of the 21st century. More than 8,200 flights were canceled on Friday evening, according to aviation data firm Cirium. And the effects continued after the ground stop was lifted, with at least another 3,000 flights canceled on Saturday.
The ground stop came just a day after the FAA announced the rollout of an AI tool for air traffic controllers; the air traffic controllers union said it was not consulted in designing the system. However, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related.”
“We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was,” Bedford said.
When Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked earlier if the ground stop was caused by AI, he replied, “We call it SI [super intelligence] around here, remember? SI.”

title_en: Work to replace old copper wire led to the FAA’s ground stop
title_fa: Work to replace old copper wire led to the FAA’s ground stop
excerpt_en: At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday's nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a "remote FAA facility." The secretary said that this was "routine...
excerpt_fa: At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday's nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a "remote FAA facility." The secretary said that this was "routine...
content_en:
At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday’s nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a “remote FAA facility.” The secretary said that this was “routine maintenance,” rather than the result of a major modernization effort. He told reporters that it was “such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down,” necessitating the upgrade.
Work to replace old copper wire led to the FAA’s ground stop
Issues with a new router related to a fiber optic upgrade grounded thousands of flights on Friday.
Issues with a new router related to a fiber optic upgrade grounded thousands of flights on Friday.
What wasn’t clear, according to Secretary Duffy, was the root cause of the problem. He said that it could have been faulty hardware, a misconfigured router, or “incompetence” on the part of contractor L3Harris. Regardless, what followed was the newly installed router “flooding” other routers in the Air Traffic Control system. Duffy said that there were “over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” causing disruption to radar feeds and communication with planes.
Secretary Duffy also took the opportunity to call on additional funding from Congress for modernizing the Air Traffic Control system, and to tout the work the FAA has done so far. “We are building, we are building safely, but we are building fast,” he said, but said that Congress had only given him a “partial payment” to complete the necessary work.
In a statement posted to their site, L3Harris said:
L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.

title_en: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
title_fa: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
excerpt_en: Some governments moved to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
excerpt_fa: Some governments moved to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
content_en:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.
Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.
China
China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday, a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.
Singapore
In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.
In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case.
South Korea
South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report.
Taiwan
Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media. Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project.
Japan
In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

content_en:
Black Friday has become a shopping season of its own, with retailers once again offering discounts well ahead of the actual shopping holiday. We’ve already rounded up some of the best early Black Friday deals we’ve come across, but if you’re looking to save on outdoor gear or pick up something for an upcoming trip, REI’s annual Holiday Sale, which runs through November 23rd, is worth checking out.
Here are our favorite deals from REI’s giant Holiday Sale
From Garmin watches to seasonal camping gear, REI is offering a slate of deep discounts ahead of Black Friday.
From Garmin watches to seasonal camping gear, REI is offering a slate of deep discounts ahead of Black Friday.
As usual, the outdoor retailer is offering discounts on everything from smartwatches to camping equipment. In some cases, we’re seeing some of the lowest prices we’ve seen on our favorite wearables, including Garmin’s Forerunner 570, while gadgets like the InReach Mini 3 are also receiving sizable discounts. REI members can also use promo code HOLIDAY2026 to save 20 percent on one full-price item, plus an additional 20 percent on one REI Outlet item.
To save you time, we’ve sifted through the deluge of discounts to find an assortment of deals we recommend here at The Verge. We’ve also noted when competing retailers are offering lower prices on the same items, so you can be sure you’re getting the best deal possible.
Featured Products
Smartwatches and fitness tech
Garmin Forerunner 570
Garmin’s Forerunner 570 features a bright OLED display, skin temperature sensors, and a built-in speaker and microphone for taking calls. It also offers multiband GPS, personalized training plans, and up to 11 days of battery life.
Garmin Venu 4
Garmin’s Venu 4 is geared toward the average athlete, offering heart rate alerts, detailed sleep insights, guided meditation, and a wheelchair mode. It also introduces caffeine and alcohol tracking, along with Garmin Coach, which tailors workouts to your fitness history, sleep, and recovery.
- REI, Amazon, and Best Buy are also selling the Garmin Lily 2 Active for $249.99 ($50 off), which is its lowest price to date. The stylish smartwatch is a great budget-friendly Garmin, especially for people with smaller wrists. Like the standard Lily 2, it offers basic fitness tracking, notifications, and up to five days of battery life; however, the so-called “Active” model adds a physical button, built-in GPS, and support for more sports tracking. Read our Lily 2 review.
- The Garmin Vivoactive 6 has returned to its all-time low of $249.99 ($50 off) at Amazon, Walmart, and REI. The fitness watch offers up to 11 days of battery life and tracks a range of workouts, including walking, running, cycling, HIIT, golf, and more. It also provides extensive health monitoring, including wrist-based heart rate detection, menstrual cycle and pregnancy tracking, and a customizable morning report that summarizes helpful health-related info. However, it lacks ECG compatibility, though it does have a slightly slimmer profile than its predecessor.
Garmin Fenix 8
The Garmin Fenix 8 is a premium multisport watch that features a speaker, mic, and on-device assistant for calls, timers, and voice commands. It also offers elite battery life, dual-frequency GPS, and robust sensors. Read our review.
- The Wahoo Kickr V6 Smart Trainer is on sale at REI for $679.99 ($170 off). Like the more affordable Kickr Core 2 we covered in July, the Kickr V6 turns your existing bike into an indoor exercise bike, with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity for pairing with apps like Zwift. However, the higher-end trainer offers up to 2,200W of resistance and can replicate inclines of up to 20 percent, compared to the Core 2’s 1,800W and 16 percent. It also provides more accurate power measurements and is designed so that indoor rides feel more natural.
Phone accessories and entertainment
EcoFlow Rapid Magnetic Power Bank
EcoFlow’s Rapid Magnetic Power Bank is a 10,000mAh Qi2 battery that can snap to the back of your device if you’re using a newer iPhone or select Android devices, thus supplying it with up to 15W of power. It also includes a built-in USB-C cable that can provide up to 65W of power to larger devices, including a 13-inch MacBook Air.
- If you own an older iPhone with a Lightning port, you can grab InfinityLab’s InstantGo 10,000 Power Bank for $41.93 (about $28 off) at REI. The portable battery features a 10,000mAh capacity and a built-in Lightning cable, making it a solid all-in-one option for days when you won’t be near an outlet. It also supports passthrough charging, so you can charge your phone and the power bank at the same time.
- DJI’s Osmo Mobile 8 is on sale for around $128.99 ($21 off) at REI, Amazon, and Best Buy, which is $10 shy of its best price to date. The smartphone gimbal supports 360-degree horizontal rotation and Apple’s DockKit, which allows the gimbal to track and follow pets and people across a wider range of camera apps. This discounted Advanced Tracking Combo also includes a multifunctional module for tracking people and pets, as well as a built-in tripod and extension rod that make it easier to film yourself without someone behind the camera.
Soundcore Liberty 5
The Soundcore Liberty 5 feature adaptive noise cancellation and support for Dolby Audio, along with six swappable tips so you can find the right fit. They also sport an IP55 rating for water and dust resistance and can last up to 48 hours with the included charging case.
- You can buy Soundcore’s AeroFit 2 for $79.99 ($20 off) at REI, Amazon, and Best Buy, which is $2 shy of their lowest price to date. Their open-ear design lets you listen to music while staying vigilant in your surroundings; they also feature adjustable ear hooks for a secure fit, IP55 water and dust resistance, and up to 42 hours of battery life with the included charging case.

content_en:
Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life.
The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
CSET’s Helen Toner says ‘we’re screwed’ if our AI safety plan rests on any one person being trusted to get this right.
Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely.
But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor.
Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble.
So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks so much. Great to be here.
I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.”
Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET?
It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019.
Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI.
Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff.
Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys.
The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.”
It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like?
It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do.
AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or...

excerpt_en: Tesla is doubling, or perhaps tripling down on its bold claims of an autonomous future with the offer to "select customers" to purchase a Cybercab for "personal use." But the gilded, steering-wheel-free two-seater will "only be available in supported service areas" - meaning...
excerpt_fa: Tesla is doubling, or perhaps tripling down on its bold claims of an autonomous future with the offer to "select customers" to purchase a Cybercab for "personal use." But the gilded, steering-wheel-free two-seater will "only be available in supported service areas" - meaning...
content_en:
Tesla is doubling, or perhaps tripling down on its bold claims of an autonomous future with the offer to “select customers” to purchase a Cybercab for “personal use.” But the gilded, steering-wheel-free two-seater will “only be available in supported service areas” — meaning you’ll only be able to buy one if you live in one of the cities where Tesla currently operates its Robotaxi service.
Tesla is inviting some people to buy a Cybercab ‘for personal use’ — but read the fine print
Look past the $29,990 sticker price and the math — and regulatory risk — gets messy fast.
Look past the $29,990 sticker price and the math — and regulatory risk — gets messy fast.
The price of a Cybercab is listed at $29,990, plus a mandatory $299-a-month “Autonomy Subscription.” Tesla’s Robotaxi account on X announced the new offer, including screenshots of the order page and the invite email. But don’t expect a fleet of personally owned Cybercabs to suddenly materialize on public roads: “Initial availability is limited,” the invitation email warns.
Tesla began offering rides in the Cybercab as part of its Model Y-powered Robotaxi service in Austin in September. The company now has 278 Cybercabs in operation, representing approximately 40 percent of its fleet, according to the crowd-sourced Robotaxi Tracker.
The inclusion of a mandatory $299/month subscription is sure to rankle some fans who may have dreamed of cruising around in a $30,000 driverless Tesla, as originally promised by Tesla CEO Elon Musk when he first introduced the Cybercab in 2024. Musk made no mention of the Autonomy Subscription at that event, though it shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise given the $99/month fee Tesla currently charges for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) feature.
Still, that money adds up over time. Over a standard 5-year ownership period, the mandatory $299/month fee adds $17,940 to the sticker price (even with the first month included), bringing the real baseline cost to roughly $47,600 before taxes, charging, and insurance — more than a brand-new Model 3 or Model Y that you can actually drive anywhere in the country.
Unlike a standard Tesla where canceling FSD just reverts the car to manual driving, canceling the $299/month Autonomy Subscription renders the Cybercab completely unusable on public roads because there is no manual fallback. In effect, the car becomes a brick. Additionally, Tesla says that buyers will have to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit just to get in line for a December delivery window that isn’t guaranteed.
One of the biggest selling points of Musk’s 2024 “We, Robot” pitch was that regular people could buy a Cybercab and add it to Tesla’s Robotaxi network to earn passive income while they sleep or work. But the order terms explicitly prohibit owners from using the vehicle for commercial purposes — meaning no Uber, no DoorDash, and no putting it on Tesla’s own Robotaxi network to offset the $299/month fee. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy has floated Q2 2027 as a possible target for letting customer cars join the network, so early buyers are paying full freight with zero way to monetize the car.
Moreover, Tesla only has to give you 30 days’ warning before raising the price. If they update the rules and you keep using the service, you automatically agree to the new terms. Also, if you cancel — or if Tesla suspends your access — you won’t get a partial refund for the rest of the month you already paid for.
Of course, that’s just the fine print. On X, Tesla CEO Elon Musk was promising a much wider rollout, subject — of course — to “regulatory approval.” Musk frequently frames regulatory approval as the primary external bottleneck holding back his robotaxi timelines as a way to shift focus away from Tesla’s technological shortcomings.
(For what it’s worth, he also called his own company’s $299/month Autonomy Subscription “too high,” arguing that it should actually be $115/month or closer to Tesla’s $99/month Full Self-Driving subscription.)
But Musk seemed more focused on taunting YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who promised to shave his head if Tesla delivered a Cybercab for under $30,000 before 2027, than answering any of the litany of safety and liability questions raised by this offer. (For his part, Brownlee says he thinks his hair is safe.)
For starters, how does Tesla plan on selling a vehicle that doesn’t comply with current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards that require traditional controls like steering wheels and pedals? Tesla says the Autonomy Subscription covers autonomous driving, maintenance, and towing, but explicitly excludes auto insurance. The company hasn’t explained how personal auto insurers will underwrite a car with no human driver, or how liability is split between the owner and Tesla if the vehicle causes an accident while operating autonomously. Nor has Tesla disclosed how it selects invited buyers or how many units are earmarked for private sale versus its internal fleet.
Then there is the small matter of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration already opening a formal audit into how Tesla self-certified a vehicle without a steering wheel, pedals, or side mirrors. Tesla submitted its legal justification to NHTSA in October, requested that the entire response be kept confidential, and is now taking customer deposits while NHTSA’s ruling is still pending.
Which means early buyers aren’t just paying $47,600 for a geofenced car they aren’t allowed to drive — they’re putting down non-refundable cash on a vehicle the federal government hasn’t even decided is street-legal.

title_en: This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers
title_fa: This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers
excerpt_en: As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch's Joy-Con, my family and I can't stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo's Zero 2 controllers for...
excerpt_fa: As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch's Joy-Con, my family and I can't stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo's Zero 2 controllers for...
content_en:
As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con, my family and I can’t stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo’s Zero 2 controllers for games that don’t use analog thumbsticks. I’ve spent years hunting for an alternative that pairs the size of the Zero 2 with as much of the functionality of a larger controller as I can get, and CRKD’s new Atom Plus is nearly exactly that. But if you have larger hands like I do, you may find the gamepad’s focus on portability a struggle.
This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers
Larger hands may struggle with the Atom Plus, but it squeezes a lot of functionality into an extremely tiny controller.
Larger hands may struggle with the Atom Plus, but it squeezes a lot of functionality into an extremely tiny controller.
Measuring around 3.5 inches wide, the $29.99 Atom Plus is about a half-inch smaller than the 8BitDo Zero 2 but squeezes in considerably more features and functionality. The most obvious is a pair of symmetrical analog thumbsticks with anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance technology. You also get shoulder buttons and triggers, rumble feedback, a dedicated home button, motion controls, and customization through a mobile app.
Like many third-party controllers, the Atom Plus works with multiple platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2, PCs, Android, iOS, and various smart TVs. And just like other gamepads, pairing to different devices requires putting the Atom Plus into one of several Bluetooth modes by holding down a combination of buttons at power-up, which in this case is the home button plus a specific direction on the D-pad. It’s easy to do, but never easy to remember: I frequently needed to grab the manual or quickly Google which direction I need to press when switching devices. The Atom Plus already features a bunch of technical info etched into the back of the controller, so I’d love to see these important pairing instructions included there, too. (And that goes for all multiplatform gamepads.)
I primarily tested the Atom Plus with the Nintendo Switch 2 since I mostly plan to use the controller as a travel accessory. The thumbsticks are about the same size as those on the original Switch Joy-Con, which means they’re smaller than the Switch 2’s. And while I prefer an asymmetrical layout, the Atom Plus’ sticks are very good, with a little more tension than Nintendo’s that I find actually helps with precision movements given their limited travel.
While the overall build quality feels excellent, the Atom Plus’ tiny footprint creates some compromises and challenges. The front action buttons and D-pad feel nice and squishy, but the gamepad’s controls are a little crowded. When pressing down or right on the D-pad, my thumb regularly bumps the left thumbstick. It doesn’t hinder gameplay, but I do find it an annoying distraction.
The shoulder buttons use digital microswitches, as do the triggers, which means the latter can’t be used for racing games that support analog acceleration controls. I like that the two sets of buttons on the top edge sit at slightly different heights, but I would have preferred a little more differentiation since I’ve occasionally accidentally pressed the triggers when I meant to hit the shoulder buttons.
I was impressed with the Atom Plus’ customizability, however. When paired to an accompanying mobile app, you can check the controller’s remaining charge, turn off rumble feedback, see its unique product number (by tapping your phone to an NFC chip inside the controller), and remap any of its controls. That includes the pair of dual-function shortcut levers that replicate the Switch’s plus and minus buttons and screenshot shortcut.
Those levers move up and down and cleverly reduce the number of buttons crowding the front of the Atom Plus, but they feel a little too small, which is more or less the general theme. It’s a tiny gamepad that’s great for travel or stashing in your everyday carry. But, unsurprisingly, it probably won’t find its way into your regular gaming rotation. It’s assumed that players will be willing to settle for the compromise of occasionally contorting their fingers in weird, new ways for one of the smallest fully featured controllers on the market.
I don’t think a dual-stick controller could get any smaller than the Atom Plus without making too many ergonomic compromises. So while I applaud CRKD for the careful balancing act behind the Atom Plus’ design, and would certainly recommend it for those wanting a very capable controller that’s also cheap and portable, I’m now curious how it compares to Microsoft’s recently announced Xbox Nano controller that’s “surprisingly comfortable,” according to The Verge’s Tom Warren. It’s $20 more expensive than CRKD’s and noticeably larger, but it adds analog triggers, a more spacious design, and stubby grips making it easier to hold for those of us with beefy mitts.

Like many third-party controllers, the Atom Plus works with multiple platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2, PCs, Android, iOS, and various smart TVs. And just like other gamepads, pairing to different devices requires putting the Atom Plus into one of several Bluetooth modes by holding down a combination of buttons at power-up, which in this case is the home button plus a specific direction on the D-pad. It’s easy to do, but never easy to remember: I frequently needed to grab the manual or quickly Google which direction I need to press when switching devices. The Atom Plus already features a bunch of technical info etched into the back of the controller, so I’d love to see these important pairing instructions included there, too. (And that goes for all multiplatform gamepads.)
I primarily tested the Atom Plus with the Nintendo Switch 2 since I mostly plan to use the controller as a travel accessory. The thumbsticks are about the same size as those on the original Switch Joy-Con, which means they’re smaller than the Switch 2’s. And while I prefer an asymmetrical layout, the Atom Plus’ sticks are very good, with a little more tension than Nintendo’s that I find actually helps with precision movements given their limited travel.
While the overall build quality feels excellent, the Atom Plus’ tiny footprint creates some compromises and challenges. The front action buttons and D-pad feel nice and squishy, but the gamepad’s controls are a little crowded. When pressing down or right on the D-pad, my thumb regularly bumps the left thumbstick. It doesn’t hinder gameplay, but I do find it an annoying distraction.
The shoulder buttons use digital microswitches, as do the triggers, which means the latter can’t be used for racing games that support analog acceleration controls. I like that the two sets of buttons on the top edge sit at slightly different heights, but I would have preferred a little more differentiation since I’ve occasionally accidentally pressed the triggers when I meant to hit the shoulder buttons.
I was impressed with the Atom Plus’ customizability, however. When paired to an accompanying mobile app, you can check the controller’s remaining charge, turn off rumble feedback, see its unique product number (by tapping your phone to an NFC chip inside the controller), and remap any of its controls. That includes the pair of dual-function shortcut levers that replicate the Switch’s plus and minus buttons and screenshot shortcut.
Those levers move up and down and cleverly reduce the number of buttons crowding the front of the Atom Plus, but they feel a little too small, which is more or less the general theme. It’s a tiny gamepad that’s great for travel or stashing in your everyday carry. But, unsurprisingly, it probably won’t find its way into your regular gaming rotation. It’s assumed that players will be willing to settle for the compromise of occasionally contorting their fingers in weird, new ways for one of the smallest fully featured controllers on the market.
I don’t think a dual-stick controller could get any smaller than the Atom Plus without making too many ergonomic compromises. So while I applaud CRKD for the careful balancing act behind the Atom Plus’ design, and would certainly recommend it for those wanting a very capable controller that’s also cheap and portable, I’m now curious how it compares to Microsoft’s recently announced Xbox Nano controller that’s “surprisingly comfortable,” according to The Verge’s Tom Warren. It’s $20 more expensive than CRKD’s and noticeably larger, but it adds analog triggers, a more spacious design, and stubby grips making it easier to hold for those of us with beefy mitts.
